sentences: Before us is Mount Inwang, moments after the rain has stopped.
The scroll is about 1.
38 metres wide, and a dark mass of rock fills almost all of it.
Stand back for a moment and simply feel its weight.
Jeong Seon, known as Gyeomjae, was seventy-five when he painted this.
Most painters of his day copied idealized landscapes from Chinese model books, but Jeong perfected true-view landscape, painting the actual mountains of Korea in front of him.
Now look at the great rock face in the centre.
It is built from layer upon layer of dense ink, conveying the weight of granite still dark and glistening with rain.
Broad strokes, pulled from top to bottom, are stacked across its surface.
In the upper right, the artist wrote the title, Inwang jesaek, his pen name Gyeomjae, and a date: the last days of the leap month in the sinmi year.
Scholars read this as late in the intercalary fifth month of 1751.
In the gully to the right of the peak, thin white streams pour down.
This is rainwater gathering between the rocks after days of rain.
Court weather records from late in that same leap month note several rainy days, then clearing skies.
Now follow the white mist rising around the mountain's waist.
It is not paint at all; it is simply bare paper, left untouched.
This negative space, set against heavy ink, creates the damp air of a morning after rain.
Below the mist, a forest of pines and other trees spreads out.
The leaves are short dabs of ink, and the trunks are laid down in a few quick strokes.
Unlike the heavy rock, the woods feel light and rhythmic.
Tucked into the trees at lower right is a house with a tiled roof.
Some scholars see it as the home of Yi Byeong-yeon, a poet and Jeong's old friend.
From that reading came the story that Jeong painted this hoping his sick friend would recover.
Yi did in fact die on the twenty-ninth day of that same leap month.
Yet the inscription never names him, and others argue the house does not match where he lived.
What the records do confirm is a deep friendship, shared through paintings and poems.
The painting is designated a National Treasure of Korea.
It belonged for many years to the Samsung chairman Lee Kun-hee, and in 2021 his family donated it to the National Museum of Korea.
It is counted among the high points of Joseon painting.
Step back once more and take in the whole scroll.
Look up at Inwangsan from Seoul today and you will be struck by how true it is.
Can you almost smell the wet rock and pine after the rain?
